title: The hidden gift
hook: Zhuangzi's hunchback Shu is spared the army and fed by the state (Zhuangzi 4)
carry: a side the world's measuring stick misses

segments.voice: Yesterday: hukam, the order no one is outside of. Your line was no one is outside it. What did you go with today instead of fighting? Now a new week, and a strange, funny teacher from ancient China. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

The recruiters have come to town. They're rounding up men for the army, and every young man with a strong back has found somewhere to hide: the hayloft, an aunt's house, the reeds by the river. Except one. He's strolling right down the middle of the street, arms swinging, saying hello to the officers. Nobody stops him. Nobody even looks twice. His name, in the book of Zhuangzi, is Shu, and the reason nobody drafts him is his body. Today, a story about what a limit can quietly hold.
screen: `THE RECRUITERS COME TO TOWN.` → `EVERYONE HIDES. EXCEPT ONE.` → `HIS NAME IS SHU.`

segments.voice: First, who Shu is. Zhuangzi describes him in big, almost cartoon strokes: his chin tucked down by his navel, his shoulders higher than the top of his head, his hair knot pointing at the sky. It's a body that fits none of the world's measures. Second, how he lives. He isn't helpless in the story. He earns his food sewing and washing clothes, and by sifting grain he makes enough to feed others besides himself. Third, the turn. When the army comes, he walks among the recruiters without fear. When the state calls up men for heavy labor, he's excused, because of his condition. And when the state hands out grain to the sick, he gets his share, and firewood too. Then Zhuangzi draws the lesson, in paraphrase: if a man whose body is out of the usual shape can look after himself and live out his years, how much more someone whose virtue is out of the usual shape. This whole chapter is set in a dangerous world, where being useful gets you used up. This path met the useless tree in its first year; Shu is its neighbor in the same chapter. And the chapter ends, in paraphrase: everyone knows the use of the useful, but nobody knows the use of the useless. Fourth, what it isn't. Zhuangzi doesn't say every limit is secretly a blessing, and nobody gets to tell you yours is. He turns the picture, once, to show a side the world's measuring stick misses. The gift is hidden, partial, and still real.
screen: `A BODY THAT FITS NO MEASURE.` · `HE EARNS HIS KEEP.` · `SPARED THE ARMY, FED BY THE STATE.` · `NOT A PROMISE. A TURNED PICTURE.` · then, large: `THE USE OF THE USELESS.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one limit you live with. Keep it small enough to hold today: a knee that won't run, a shyness, no car, not enough money for the thing everyone else is doing. Hold it without arguing with it. Then ask it two quiet questions. What do you spare me from? And what do you leave room for? Maybe something comes: a slower walk where you notice more, an evening you didn't have to be anywhere. Maybe nothing comes, and that's an honest answer too. The bell holds the time.
Shu, the man in Zhuangzi whose body didn't fit the world's measure, and who was spared and fed because of it. Today's word.

Your line: a side the world's measuring stick misses. Today, when a limit gets in your way, ask it once what it spares you, and let the answer be small, or nothing at all. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi, Daoists among them, read Shu and the useless tree together as stories about the use of the useless, and some return to them in times of illness, disability or failure.

original.note: classical Chinese, from the end of Zhuangzi chapter 4: the use of the useless (wú yòng zhī yòng).

trapdoor: what you thought: a feel-good story: every weakness is really a strength.
what it means: in a world that uses up the useful, a limit can quietly protect someone; Zhuangzi turns the picture without promising anything.
what a scholar hears: Zhuangzi chapter 4, the human world, where Shu and the useless tree sit side by side, and which ends on the use of the useless.

sources.ref: Zhuangzi 4 (closing lines: the use of the useless)

notes: Zhuangzi 4 paraphrased from the Chinese and Legge (1891), not quoted: Shu's body (chin hidden at the navel, shoulders above the head, hair knot pointing to the sky); he earns his food sewing and washing, and by winnowing grain feeds ten people (the number is cut); spared the draft and corvee labor; receives grain and ten bundles of firewood when the state relieves the sick (numbers cut). Confirm.

Zhuangzi's moral paraphrased: if one whose body is 'out of shape' (支離其形) can care for himself and finish his years, how much more one whose virtue is 'out of shape' (支離其德). Confirm the rendering 'out of the usual shape'.
Closing line of chapter 4: 人皆知有用之用，而莫知無用之用也, paraphrased. Confirm.
Disability: the story is Zhuangzi's comic exaggeration. The script says plainly that nobody gets to call another person's limit a blessing; a reviewer should confirm the tone is respectful.
The useless tree (Carpenter Shi's oak) was day 52; this day only names it as a neighbor in the same chapter.
Opening scene (recruiters, hiding places) is the script's dramatization of the text's single line about the draft; the hayloft and reeds are invented color.
Audit: fork setup no longer states as text that every young man hid; that is the hook's invented color, not Zhuangzi's.
